blocks.text: Economics is the study of how people, firms, and governments make choices when resources are scarce — and how those choices add up across an entire society. Because you can never have everything, every decision means giving something else up.
Rule of thumb: whenever you make a decision, ask “compared to what?” That question is the whole subject in miniature.

check.question: Why does this section say every decision means giving something up?
options: Because most decisions cost money.
Because resources are scarce, so choosing one option rules out another.
Because people are bad at planning ahead.
check.explain: Scarcity is the reason. If resources were unlimited you could have everything, and nothing would be forgone.

items: Scarcity forces trade-offs: every choice carries an opportunity cost — the value of the next best thing you gave up.
Microeconomics zooms in on single markets, firms, and households; macroeconomics zooms out to the whole economy.
Incentives drive behaviour — change the costs and benefits, and you change what people do.
Models are deliberate simplifications: they trade some realism for the clarity to reason about cause and effect.

check.question: Opportunity cost is the value of what?
options: Everything you didn't choose, added together.
The next best thing you gave up.
The money you actually handed over.
check.explain: Only the single best alternative counts — not the sum of all the others, and not the cash you spent.

blocks.text: Imagine you have a free Saturday. You could work a shift for $80, study for an exam, or relax. Economics doesn't tell you which is “right” — it tells you to weigh each option against what you give up. If you choose to relax, the opportunity cost is the $80 you didn't earn plus the exam marks you didn't gain. Naming that cost is what turns a vague feeling into a clear decision.

check.question: You skip an $80 shift and an exam revision session in order to relax. What is the opportunity cost of relaxing?
options: Nothing — you didn't spend any money.
The $80 you didn't earn plus the exam marks you didn't gain.
The $80 only, since marks aren't money.
check.explain: Opportunity cost counts everything you gave up, whether or not it was cash. Naming it turns a vague feeling into a clear decision.

blocks.text: Economics is a way of thinking, not a pile of facts. Once you start spotting scarcity, trade-offs, and incentives in everyday life, the rest of the course is just adding precision to instincts you already have.

check.question: Which best matches the section's closing point?
options: Economics is a body of facts to memorise before the exam.
Economics is a way of thinking that adds precision to instincts you already have.
Economics is really a branch of mathematics.
check.explain: The section frames the rest of the course as sharpening instincts you already have about scarcity, trade-offs and incentives.

blocks.text: Economics is about making choices precise — and so is code. Edit the snippet below and press Run to see the output. Try changing the numbers.

check.question: In the snippet, wageFromShift is 80 and valueOfResting is 60. What does it print as the opportunity cost of resting?
check.explain: It prints the difference: 80 − 60 = 20, the net value given up by resting instead of working the shift.

blocks.text: Work top-to-bottom or jump straight to a topic in the sidebar. Folders expand to reveal sub-topics, and each lesson is short enough to finish in one sitting.

check.question: How is this course meant to be worked through?
options: Strictly in order, first lesson to last.
Either top-to-bottom or by jumping straight to a topic in the sidebar.
Only by searching for what you need.
check.explain: Both routes work — lessons are short enough to finish in one sitting either way.

items: Open a folder to reveal its lessons; the arrow shows whether a section is expanded.
The lesson you are reading is highlighted in the sidebar so you never lose your place.
Every lesson ends with a “Key ideas” recap — skim these to revise quickly before a test.

check.question: What does this section suggest as the quickest way to revise before a test?
options: Re-read every lesson in full.
Skim each lesson's “Key ideas” recap.
Do the practice problems only.
check.explain: Every lesson ends with a Key ideas recap, which is built for exactly this kind of fast revision.

blocks.text: A quick reference for the vocabulary that shows up again and again. Come back here whenever a term stops making sense.

check.question: How is this glossary meant to be used?
options: Memorise it all before starting the course.
Come back to it whenever a term stops making sense.
Read it once at the end.
check.explain: It's a quick reference for vocabulary that keeps recurring, not a lesson to be learned in one go.

items: Opportunity cost — the value of the best alternative you gave up.
Marginal — the effect of one more unit (one more hour, one more slice).
Equilibrium — a state with no pressure to change; supply meets demand.
Ceteris paribus — “all else equal”, the assumption that lets us isolate one cause.

check.question: What does “ceteris paribus” mean?
options: All else equal.
Other things being unequal.
At the margin.
check.explain: It's the assumption that everything else is held constant, which is what lets you isolate one cause.

blocks.text: All else equal, as the price of a good rises the quantity people want to buy falls — and as price falls, quantity demanded rises. That inverse relationship is why demand curves slope downward.

check.question: All else equal, when the price of a good rises, quantity demanded does what?
options: Rises.
Falls.
Stays the same.
check.explain: That inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded is exactly why demand curves slope downward.

items: A price change moves you along the demand curve; a change in tastes, income, or the price of related goods shifts the whole curve.
The substitution effect: when something gets pricier, buyers switch to alternatives.
The income effect: a higher price makes buyers effectively poorer, so they buy less.

check.question: A change in the good's OWN price causes what?
options: A shift of the whole demand curve.
A movement along the demand curve.
Both at once.
check.explain: Only the good's own price moves you along the curve. Tastes, income and related-goods prices shift the whole curve.

blocks.text: A coffee shop raises a latte from $4 to $5. The next morning, a handful of regulars switch to filter coffee or skip the second cup — quantity demanded falls. Nothing about the customers changed; only the price did, so we slide up the same demand curve rather than shifting it. If instead a viral post made lattes trendy, the whole curve would shift right and more would sell at every price.

check.question: A latte goes from $4 to $5 and some regulars switch to filter coffee. What has happened?
options: The demand curve shifted left.
We moved along the same demand curve.
The supply curve shifted right.
check.explain: Nothing about the customers changed — only the price — so this is a slide up the same curve, not a shift of it.

blocks.text: Always separate a movement along the curve (caused by the good's own price) from a shift of the curve (caused by anything else). Mixing them up is the single most common mistake in intro microeconomics.

check.question: What does this section call the single most common mistake in intro microeconomics?
options: Confusing supply with demand.
Confusing a movement along the curve with a shift of the curve.
Forgetting to say “ceteris paribus”.
check.explain: Always ask what changed: the good's own price (movement) or anything else (shift).

blocks.text: As the price of a good rises, producers are willing and able to supply more of it, because higher prices cover higher marginal costs and promise more profit. Supply curves therefore slope upward.

check.question: Why do supply curves slope upward?
options: Because higher prices cover higher marginal costs and promise more profit.
Because producers always prefer selling more.
Because costs fall as the price rises.
check.explain: A higher price makes additional, more expensive units worth producing — so quantity supplied rises with price.

items: Higher price → larger quantity supplied (a movement along the curve).
Costs, technology, and the number of sellers shift the entire supply curve.
In the short run, firms expand output by working existing capacity harder.

check.question: Which of these shifts the whole supply curve rather than moving along it?
options: The good's own price rising.
A new technology that cuts production costs.
Buyers wanting more of the good.
check.explain: Costs, technology and the number of sellers shift the entire curve; the good's own price only moves you along it.

blocks.text: Equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers want exactly equals the quantity sellers offer. There is no shortage and no surplus, so there is no pressure for the price to move.

check.question: What is true at market equilibrium?
options: A small surplus remains, which keeps the price stable.
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there's no pressure on price.
Supply always exceeds demand slightly.
check.explain: With no shortage and no surplus, nothing pushes the price in either direction.

items: Above equilibrium: a surplus builds up and pushes the price down.
Below equilibrium: a shortage forms and pulls the price up.
Shifts in supply or demand create a new equilibrium price and quantity.

check.question: If the price sits ABOVE equilibrium, what happens?
options: A shortage forms and pulls the price up.
A surplus builds up and pushes the price down.
Nothing — the price stays where it is.
check.explain: Above equilibrium sellers offer more than buyers want, so the unsold surplus drives the price back down.

blocks.text: Price elasticity of demand measures how sensitive quantity demanded is to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price.

check.question: How is price elasticity of demand calculated?
options: Change in quantity ÷ change in price, in units.
Percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price.
Price ÷ quantity.
check.explain: Using percentages is what makes the measure independent of the units the good is sold in.

items: Elastic (>1): quantity reacts a lot — think holidays or a specific brand of coffee.
Inelastic (<1): quantity barely moves — think petrol or insulin.
Total revenue rises when you cut the price of an elastic good, and falls for an inelastic one.

check.question: Cutting the price of a good with ELASTIC demand does what to total revenue?
options: Raises it.
Lowers it.
Leaves it unchanged.
check.explain: Demand is responsive, so the extra quantity sold more than makes up for the lower price per unit.

blocks.text: Income elasticity measures how demand responds when incomes change — the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.

check.question: Income elasticity measures how demand responds to a change in what?
options: The good's own price.
Consumer income.
The price of another good.
check.explain: It's the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.

items: Normal goods have positive income elasticity: richer buyers want more.
Luxury goods have elasticity above 1 — demand grows faster than income.
Inferior goods have negative elasticity: demand falls as income rises.

check.question: A good whose demand FALLS as income rises is called what?
options: A luxury good.
An inferior good.
A normal good.
check.explain: Inferior goods have negative income elasticity — buyers trade up to something else as they get richer.

blocks.text: Cross-price elasticity measures how the demand for one good responds to a price change in another good — revealing whether two goods are substitutes or complements.

check.question: Cross-price elasticity reveals whether two goods are what?
options: Normal or inferior.
Substitutes or complements.
Elastic or inelastic.
check.explain: It measures how demand for one good responds to a price change in another, which is exactly what that relationship is.

items: Positive value → substitutes (tea and coffee).
Negative value → complements (printers and ink).
Near zero → the two goods are basically unrelated.

check.question: Printers and ink have a negative cross-price elasticity. That makes them what?
options: Substitutes.
Complements.
Unrelated goods.
check.explain: A negative value means a price rise in one cuts demand for the other — they're bought together.

blocks.text: Utility is a way to describe the satisfaction a person gets from consuming goods. Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit — and it usually shrinks the more you already have.

check.question: What is marginal utility?
options: The total satisfaction from everything you consume.
The extra satisfaction from one more unit.
Satisfaction divided by price.
check.explain: And it usually shrinks the more of something you already have.

items: Diminishing marginal utility: the second slice of pizza delights you less than the first.
Consumers maximise utility by equalising marginal utility per dollar across goods.
It explains why demand curves slope down — extra units are worth less, so you'll only buy them at a lower price.

check.question: How does diminishing marginal utility help explain a downward-sloping demand curve?
options: Extra units are worth less to you, so you'll only buy them at a lower price.
Because supply rises when price rises.
Because incomes fall as prices rise.
check.explain: If the second unit delights you less than the first, it takes a lower price to make it worth buying.

blocks.text: An indifference curve joins all the combinations of two goods that leave a consumer equally satisfied. Together with a budget line, it shows the best bundle a consumer can afford.

check.question: Every point on a single indifference curve represents what?
options: The same total spending.
The same level of satisfaction.
The same quantity of both goods.
check.explain: That's what makes the consumer indifferent between them — the bundles differ, the satisfaction doesn't.

items: Curves further from the origin represent higher satisfaction.
Their slope — the marginal rate of substitution — is how much of one good you'll swap for the other.
The optimal choice sits where the budget line just touches the highest reachable curve.

check.question: Where does the consumer's optimal bundle sit?
options: Where the budget line crosses the origin.
Where the budget line just touches the highest reachable indifference curve.
Where two indifference curves cross.
check.explain: Curves further from the origin mean more satisfaction, so you go as far out as the budget line allows.

blocks.text: A budget constraint shows every combination of goods a consumer can buy with a given income and set of prices. It draws the boundary between what's affordable and what isn't.

check.question: What does a budget constraint show?
options: Which bundle the consumer wants most.
Every combination of goods affordable at a given income and set of prices.
The cheapest bundle available.
check.explain: It draws the boundary between what's affordable and what isn't — it says nothing about preferences.

items: The slope reflects the relative price of the two goods.
More income shifts the line outward; a price change pivots it.
Consumers choose the affordable bundle that reaches their highest indifference curve.

check.question: What does an increase in income do to the budget line?
options: Pivots it around one axis.
Shifts it outward.
Leaves it unchanged.
check.explain: More income moves the whole line out; a change in one price is what pivots it.

blocks.text: Firms pay fixed costs that don't change with output and variable costs that do. Understanding how average and marginal costs behave is the key to deciding how much to produce.

check.question: Which kind of cost does NOT change with output?
options: Variable cost.
Fixed cost.
Marginal cost.
check.explain: Fixed costs are paid regardless of how much the firm produces; variable costs move with output.

items: Marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit.
Average total cost is typically U-shaped as output grows.
A firm expands output while the extra revenue exceeds the extra (marginal) cost.

check.question: A firm should keep expanding output while what is true?
options: Average cost is still falling.
The extra revenue from a unit exceeds its marginal cost.
Fixed costs have not yet been covered.
check.explain: Every unit that brings in more than it costs to make adds to profit.

blocks.text: Revenue is price times quantity; profit is revenue minus total cost. Firms maximise profit by producing where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

check.question: Profit is maximised at the output where what holds?
options: Revenue is at its highest.
Marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Average cost is at its lowest.
check.explain: MR = MC is the profit-maximising rule, and it holds in every market structure.

items: Economic profit counts opportunity cost, not just accounting cost.
MR = MC is the profit-maximising rule in every market structure.
If price falls below average variable cost, a firm shuts down in the short run.

check.question: What distinguishes economic profit from accounting profit?
options: Economic profit also counts opportunity cost.
Economic profit ignores fixed costs.
Economic profit is always the larger of the two.
check.explain: Accounting profit only subtracts money actually spent; economic profit also subtracts what you gave up to do this instead.

blocks.text: Economies of scale exist when producing more lowers the average cost per unit — through bulk buying, specialised labour, or spreading fixed costs over more output.

check.question: Economies of scale mean that as output rises, what falls?
options: Total cost.
Average cost per unit.
Marginal revenue.
check.explain: Bulk buying, specialised labour and spreading fixed costs over more units all cut the cost of each one.

items: Internal economies come from the firm's own growth; external ones come from the whole industry.
Beyond a point, diseconomies of scale set in as coordination gets harder.
They help explain why some industries are dominated by a few large firms.

check.question: What does this section say happens beyond a certain size?
options: Economies of scale keep growing indefinitely.
Diseconomies of scale set in as coordination gets harder.
Fixed costs disappear entirely.
check.explain: Size stops paying once the firm becomes harder to coordinate than the savings are worth.

blocks.text: A perfectly competitive market has many small firms selling identical products, with free entry and full information. No single firm can influence the price — they are all price takers.

check.question: In perfect competition, an individual firm is what?
options: A price maker.
A price taker.
A monopolist.
check.explain: With many small firms selling identical products, no single firm can move the market price.

items: Firms produce where price equals marginal cost.
In the long run, free entry drives economic profit to zero.
It's a benchmark for efficiency, rarely seen exactly in the real world.

check.question: In the long run, what does free entry do to economic profit here?
options: Drives it to zero.
Raises it steadily.
Has no effect on it.
check.explain: Any profit attracts new entrants, and their competition competes that profit away.

blocks.text: A monopoly is the single seller of a product with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry. It sets price above marginal cost, producing less than a competitive market would.

check.question: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly typically does what?
options: Charges less and produces more.
Charges more and produces less.
Charges and produces roughly the same.
check.explain: It sets price above marginal cost, which means producing less than a competitive market would.

items: Monopolists are price makers, not price takers.
They earn long-run profit because entry is blocked.
The trade-off: higher prices and lower output, but sometimes more R&D.

check.question: Why can a monopoly keep earning profit in the long run?
options: Because its costs are always lower.
Because barriers to entry block competitors from entering.
Because demand for its product is always inelastic.
check.explain: In perfect competition entry competes profit away; a monopoly is protected precisely because entry is blocked.

blocks.text: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few interdependent firms. Because each one's best move depends on the others', economists analyse them with game theory.

check.question: Why do economists analyse oligopoly using game theory?
options: Because the market has very many tiny firms.
Because each firm's best move depends on what the others do.
Because prices in these markets are set by law.
check.explain: A few firms, each interdependent — that mutual second-guessing is what game theory is built to handle.

items: Firms may collude to raise prices — or compete fiercely and trigger price wars.
The kinked demand curve helps explain sticky oligopoly prices.
See The prisoner's dilemma for why cooperation is hard to sustain.

check.question: The kinked demand curve is used to explain what?
options: Why oligopoly prices tend to be sticky.
Why monopolies invest in R&D.
Why supply curves slope upward.
check.explain: It's the standard account of why firms in an oligopoly leave their prices unchanged even as costs move.

blocks.text: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period. It's the headline measure of the size of an economy.

check.question: What does GDP count?
options: Every transaction, including second-hand sales.
The market value of final goods and services produced in a period.
Government spending only.
check.explain: It's the headline measure of the size of an economy — output produced within a country over a given period.

items: Real GDP strips out inflation so you can compare years fairly.
It can be measured three ways: output, income, and expenditure — all should agree.
GDP ignores unpaid work, inequality, and environmental costs, so it's an incomplete measure of wellbeing.

check.question: What does real GDP do that nominal GDP does not?
options: Includes unpaid work.
Strips out inflation so different years compare fairly.
Counts exports only.
check.explain: Without that adjustment, rising prices alone would look like a growing economy.

blocks.text: When the news says an economy “grew 2.5% last quarter”, that figure is the change in real GDP. Economists watch it to date recessions (two straight quarters of falling real GDP is a common rule of thumb) and to compare living standards across countries by dividing GDP by population — GDP per capita.

check.question: What is the common rule of thumb for dating a recession?
options: Any quarter in which prices fall.
Two straight quarters of falling real GDP.
Unemployment rising above 5%.
check.explain: It's a rough convention rather than an official definition, but it's the one usually quoted.

blocks.text: GDP is the best single number we have for the size of an economy, but treat it as a thermometer, not a report card: it measures output, not happiness, fairness, or sustainability.

check.question: How does the summary say GDP should be treated?
options: As a report card on a country's wellbeing.
As a thermometer — it measures output, not happiness, fairness or sustainability.
As a precise measure of inequality.
check.explain: It's the best single number for the size of an economy, and a poor one for how well people are living.

blocks.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which erodes the purchasing power of money. It's usually tracked with the Consumer Price Index, a basket of typical household goods.

check.question: Inflation erodes what?
options: The purchasing power of money.
The number of goods an economy can produce.
The exchange rate, and nothing else.
check.explain: A sustained rise in the general price level means each unit of currency buys less than it did.

items: Demand-pull inflation comes from too much spending; cost-push from rising input costs.
Moderate, stable inflation (around 2%) is generally seen as healthy.
Deflation — falling prices — can be as damaging as high inflation.

check.question: Inflation driven by rising input costs is called what?
options: Demand-pull inflation.
Cost-push inflation.
Deflation.
check.explain: Demand-pull comes from too much spending; cost-push comes from the supply side, as inputs get dearer.

blocks.text: The unemployment rate is the share of the labour force that is willing and able to work but cannot find a job. It comes in several types with very different causes.

check.question: The unemployment rate counts people who are what?
options: Not working, for any reason at all.
Willing and able to work but unable to find a job.
Working fewer hours than they would like.
check.explain: Someone who isn't looking for work isn't in the labour force, so they don't appear in the rate.

items: Frictional: people between jobs. Structural: skills don't match available jobs.
Cyclical unemployment rises during recessions.
There's often a short-run trade-off between unemployment and inflation (the Phillips curve).

check.question: Unemployment caused by workers' skills not matching available jobs is which type?
options: Frictional.
Structural.
Cyclical.
check.explain: Frictional is the gap between jobs; cyclical rises in recessions; structural is the skills mismatch.

blocks.text: Fiscal policy is the government's use of spending and taxation to influence the economy. Spending more or taxing less stimulates demand; the reverse cools an overheating economy.

check.question: Fiscal policy is the government's use of what?
options: Interest rates and the money supply.
Spending and taxation.
Exchange rate pegs.
check.explain: Interest rates and the money supply are monetary policy, run by the central bank.

items: Expansionary policy fights recessions but can widen the deficit.
The multiplier: one dollar of government spending can raise total output by more than a dollar.
Automatic stabilisers (like unemployment benefits) act without new legislation.

check.question: What makes automatic stabilisers automatic?
options: They need new legislation each time they're used.
They act without new legislation.
They only operate during booms.
check.explain: Something like unemployment benefit rises as soon as a downturn starts, with no new decision required.

blocks.text: Monetary policy is how a central bank manages interest rates and the money supply to keep inflation and employment on target. It's the main day-to-day tool for steering the economy.

check.question: Who runs monetary policy?
options: The government's treasury department.
The central bank.
Commercial banks, collectively.
check.explain: And central banks are usually independent of the government, which is what protects the inflation target.

items: Lower rates encourage borrowing and spending; higher rates restrain them.
Central banks are usually independent of the government.
Quantitative easing injects money directly when rates are already near zero.

check.question: When is quantitative easing typically used?
options: When inflation is running very high.
When interest rates are already near zero.
When the currency is pegged.
check.explain: Once rates can't usefully go lower, the central bank injects money directly instead.

blocks.text: A country has a comparative advantage in whatever it can produce at the lowest opportunity cost. Even a country that's worse at everything gains by specialising and trading.

check.question: A country has a comparative advantage in whatever it can produce at what?
options: The lowest absolute cost.
The lowest opportunity cost.
The highest quality.
check.explain: It's about what you give up to make something — not whether you're better at it than anyone else.

items: It's about relative cost, not absolute skill.
Specialisation plus trade lets both partners consume beyond their own limits.
It's the core argument for why free trade can make everyone better off.

check.question: Can a country that is worse at producing everything still gain from trade?
options: No — it has nothing worth offering.
Yes — the gains come from relative, not absolute, cost.
Only if it has natural resources to sell.
check.explain: Specialising where your opportunity cost is lowest lets both partners consume beyond their own limits.

blocks.text: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. It shapes the cost of imports and exports and can be set by markets or managed by governments.

check.question: An exchange rate is what?
options: The interest rate charged on foreign loans.
The price of one currency in terms of another.
The balance of trade between two countries.
check.explain: That price is what shapes the cost of imports and exports.

items: A weaker currency makes exports cheaper and imports dearer.
Floating rates move with supply and demand; fixed rates are pegged.
Interest rates, trade balances, and expectations all push rates around.

check.question: A weaker domestic currency makes what happen?
options: Exports cheaper and imports dearer.
Exports dearer and imports cheaper.
No difference to either.
check.explain: Foreign buyers need less of their own currency to buy your goods, while imports take more of yours.

blocks.text: Behavioral economics studies the systematic ways real people depart from the “perfectly rational” actor of standard theory. Cognitive biases are the predictable mental shortcuts behind those departures.

check.question: What does behavioral economics study?
options: The random mistakes people make by accident.
The systematic, predictable ways people depart from perfect rationality.
How firms decide what to charge.
check.explain: The departures are patterned, which is what makes them worth modelling at all.

items: Loss aversion: losses hurt about twice as much as equivalent gains feel good.
Anchoring: the first number you see quietly shapes your later judgements.
Present bias: we over-value rewards now and under-save for later.

check.question: Loss aversion means that losses do what?
options: Feel about the same as equivalent gains.
Hurt about twice as much as equivalent gains feel good.
Are generally ignored by decision-makers.
check.explain: That asymmetry is why people cling to what they already have far more than standard theory predicts.

blocks.text: A nudge changes the way choices are presented — without banning options or changing incentives — to steer people toward better decisions. The design of those options is called choice architecture.

check.question: What makes something a nudge rather than a regulation?
options: It bans the worse option outright.
It changes how choices are presented, without banning options or changing incentives.
It taxes the worse option.
check.explain: Bans and taxes change the options or their costs; a nudge only changes how they're laid out.

items: Defaults are powerful: automatic pension enrolment dramatically raises saving.
Good nudges are transparent and easy to opt out of.
Small framing changes can produce large behavioural effects.

check.question: Which example does this section give of a powerful nudge?
options: A tax on sugary drinks.
Automatic enrolment into a pension.
Banning cigarette advertising.
check.explain: Defaults are powerful precisely because most people never change them — so the default choice becomes most people's choice.

blocks.text: The prisoner's dilemma is the classic game showing why two rational players might fail to cooperate even when cooperation would leave them both better off. It underpins much of game theory.

check.question: What does the prisoner's dilemma show?
options: That cooperation always wins in the end.
That two rational players can fail to cooperate even when both would be better off.
That people rarely behave rationally.
check.explain: Both players reason perfectly well and still end up somewhere worse than if they'd cooperated.

items: Each player's dominant strategy is to defect — so both do, and both lose.
It explains arms races, price wars, and why cartels break down.
Repeating the game can sustain cooperation through reputation and retaliation.

check.question: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, each player's dominant strategy is what?
options: To cooperate.
To defect.
To pick at random.
check.explain: Defecting is better whatever the other does — so both defect, and both end up worse off.

blocks.text: Two rival petrol stations on the same corner both “know” they'd earn more if they kept prices high. But each is tempted to undercut the other by a cent to steal customers — so both cut, and both end up with thin margins. That's the prisoner's dilemma playing out on the street: individually rational moves lead to a collectively worse outcome.

check.question: Two petrol stations both undercut each other and end up on thin margins. Why is this a prisoner's dilemma?
options: Because they agreed in advance to cut prices.
Because each acting in its own interest leaves both worse off.
Because customers end up paying more.
check.explain: Each cut is individually rational — steal the customers — but the pair of rational moves is collectively worse.

blocks.text: Whenever you see cooperation that “should” happen but doesn't — climate agreements, doping in sport, ad spending wars — look for a prisoner's dilemma underneath. The fix is almost always to change the payoffs or repeat the game.

check.question: According to the summary, the fix is almost always to do what?
options: Add more players to the game.
Change the payoffs, or repeat the game.
Regulate the price directly.
check.explain: Repetition lets reputation and retaliation do the work; changing payoffs removes the temptation to defect.

blocks.text: The formulas you'll reach for most often, gathered in one place.

check.question: GDP by the expenditure method is which of these?

Investment in non-current assets and working capital is deducted after operating profit, so a year of heavy capital spending can swallow a rising profit. Depreciation is added back rather than deducted, and dividends are paid out of free cash flow — they sit after it, not inside it.
options: It spent heavily on new plant and on stock, so the cash went into those rather than to investors
Its depreciation charge increased, which reduced the cash available
It paid a larger dividend, which is deducted in arriving at free cash flow
Free cash flow cannot fall in a year when operating profit rises
check.question: A company’s operating profit rose from ZMW4 million to ZMW6 million, but its free cash flow fell over the same year. What best explains that?

blocks.text: Free cash flow is the cash a business has left after it has paid its operating costs and its tax, and made the investment it needs to keep trading and to grow. Nobody inside the business has a further claim on it, which is what makes it free — it can go to the people who funded the business.

That is why it tells you more than profit does. Profit is struck after non-cash charges like depreciation and before the capital spending that keeps the machinery running, so it can move in one direction while the bank balance moves in the other. Cash cannot. A company can report a rising operating profit for three years and still run out of money.

The gap is easy to see in a Zambian milling business. It sells maize meal to wholesalers on 60-day credit, books the revenue and the profit the day the truck leaves, and then has to find cash for the ZESCO bill, the fuel and the next consignment of grain before a single customer has paid. The profit is real. The cash is somewhere else.
Free cash flow is what a business could hand to its investors without damaging its ability to keep trading.

check.explain: Free cash flow to the firm measures what the whole business generates for everyone who funded it. Interest is a payment to one of those groups, so it comes off only when you go a step further and work out free cash flow to equity.
options: Free cash flow to the firm is the cash available to lenders and shareholders together, so paying the lenders first would understate it
Interest is a non-cash charge, so it is added back alongside depreciation
Interest has already been taken off in arriving at profit before interest and tax
Interest is relieved against tax, so deducting it as well would be double-counting
check.question: Interest paid is not deducted when you calculate free cash flow to the firm. Why not?

blocks.text: You build free cash flow out of the accounts. Start at operating profit before interest and tax, then correct it for everything the accounts recorded on a basis other than cash.

rows: Operating profit before interest and tax (PBIT)
Less replacement investment in non-current assets
Less incremental investment in non-current assets
Less incremental investment in working capital

items: Depreciation is added back because no money moved. It is the accounts spreading the cost of an asset over its life, not a payment made this year.
Tax is deducted at the amount actually paid, because that money genuinely leaves.
Replacement investment keeps the existing assets working. A business that stops replacing them is quietly shrinking, so this spending is not optional.
Incremental investment in non-current assets buys the extra capacity that growth needs.
Incremental working capital is the stock and the receivables that growth ties up before any customer pays.

blocks.text: Interest is nowhere in that working, and its absence is the point. This is cash to the firm as a whole — to lenders and shareholders together. Deducting interest here would pay one group of investors before you had finished measuring what there is to share.

blocks.text: New borrowing is added rather than ignored. It is cash arriving in the business that the shareholders can use this year, even though it will have to be serviced and repaid later. A company that repays ZMW30 million of old loans and draws down ZMW30 million of new ones has moved no cash at all, and the working should say so.
Because it is the shareholders’ cash, free cash flow to equity is the honest way to test whether a dividend is affordable.
Cash dividend cover  =  FCFE ÷ D
where: FCFE = free cash flow to equity for the year
D = dividends actually paid to shareholders in the year

blocks.text: A cover of 2 means the company generated twice the cash it handed out. Below 1 means it paid dividends it had not earned in cash, and funded the difference from reserves or from borrowing. The same company measured on earnings can look comfortable, because earnings never had the capital spending taken out of them.
Cash to the firm answers what the business generates. Cash to equity answers what the shareholders can actually be paid.

blocks.text: Free cash flow does three jobs, and which of the two measures you reach for follows from the job in front of you.

items: Appraising a project — the free cash flows the project itself generates are what get discounted to find its net present value.

Reading a company’s health — a business whose free cash flow has turned negative while its profit holds up is the classic early warning, which is why the measure is central to work on corporate failure and reconstruction.
Valuing a business — the value of a company is the present value of the free cash flows it will produce, so this is where a share price comes from.

rows: What is the whole business worth?

blocks.text: The pairing is not a convention to memorise — it is a matching rule. Cash that belongs to everybody is discounted at a rate that reflects what everybody demands. Cash that belongs to shareholders alone is discounted at what shareholders alone demand. Mixing them values a company at a number nobody could ever collect. Where those two rates come from is the whole of Lesson 2.

check.explain: An extra ZMW40,000 tied up in stock and receivables is ZMW40,000 that did not reach anybody, so both measures drop by the full amount: the firm to ZMW165,000 and equity to ZMW140,000. Working capital is very much a cash item — it is cash sitting in the warehouse instead of the bank.

It stays at ZMW180,000, because working capital is not a cash item
It falls to ZMW165,000

check.question: A project will pay ZMW500,000 in three years. The cost of capital is 10%. What is that worth today?

blocks.text: ZMW1,000 in your hand today is worth more than ZMW1,000 promised in a year. You could put today’s money to work, and the promise might not be kept. Before you can add up cash flows that arrive in different years, you have to restate them all in today’s money.

That restatement is discounting, and the rate you discount at is the company’s cost of capital — what its investors demand for leaving their money in the business. Multiply a future cash flow by its discount factor and you have its present value.
Discount factor  =  1 ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ
where: r = the cost of capital, written as a decimal
n = the number of years until the cash flow arrives

blocks.text: At a cost of capital of 10%, a kwacha due in one year is worth 1 ÷ 1.10 = 0.909 today, and one due in two years is worth 1 ÷ 1.10² = 0.826. The factor falls every year, which is the arithmetic saying what everyone already knows: the further away the money, the less you should pay for it now.

blocks.note: Cash at year 0 is already in today’s money, so its factor is 1.000.

sections.heading: Why a future kwacha is worth less

check.explain: When you must pick one, take the larger NPV — the objective is to add the most value, not the highest return per kwacha. Return per kwacha only becomes the deciding test when capital is rationed, which is a later step. And they cannot both be taken; they are mutually exclusive.
options: Project A, because it adds more value to the business
Project B, because it earns more per kwacha invested
Both, since both have positive NPVs
Neither can be chosen without knowing the payback periods
check.question: Two mutually exclusive projects are appraised at the same cost of capital. Project A has an NPV of ZMW400,000; Project B has an NPV of ZMW250,000 on half the initial outlay. Which should the company take?

blocks.text: Net present value is the sum of the present values of every cash flow a project causes, including the money you spend at the start. It answers one question: does this project make the owners of the business richer, and by how much in today’s money?
NPV  =  Σ  CFₙ ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ  −  I₀
where: CFₙ = the net cash flow the project generates in year n
r = the cost of capital used to discount
n = the year in which the cash flow arrives
I₀ = the amount invested at the start, in year 0

items: A positive NPV means the project earns more than the cost of the money funding it. Accept it.
A negative NPV means it earns less. The business would be better off leaving the money where it is.
An NPV of zero means it earns exactly the required return — no better, no worse than the alternative.

blocks.text: The number itself is meaningful, not just its sign. An NPV of ZMW1,967 says the project is worth ZMW1,967 more than it costs, in today’s money, after paying every provider of capital what they demanded.
NPV is the amount by which a project increases the value of the business, measured today.

check.explain: Year 0 is today. Discounting exists to bring future money back to the present, and this money is already there. Outflows in later years are discounted exactly like inflows.
options: Because it is already in today’s money, so there is nothing to discount
Because outflows are never discounted, only inflows are
Because the discount factor for the first year is always 1.000
Because the project has not started earning, so the cost of capital does not yet apply
check.question: In the working above, why does the year 0 outflow carry a discount factor of 1.000?

blocks.text: A project needs ZMW24,000 up front and will generate cash over five years. The cost of capital is 10%. Lay the years out in a column, discount each one, and add up.
The NPV is positive, so the project is worth doing: it returns the ZMW24,000, pays the 10% the providers of capital require on it, and leaves ZMW1,967 of value over.

Notice how the answer is built. The initial outlay sits at year 0 at a factor of 1.000, because it is spent today and needs no discounting. Every other line is a forecast cash flow multiplied by its factor. There is no arithmetic in an NPV harder than that — the difficulty in an exam is always in deciding which cash flows belong in the table at all.

check.explain: The tests answer different questions. NPV asks whether the project is worth more than it costs; discounted payback asks how long the company is exposed before it gets its money back. A project can easily create value slowly.
options: It creates value, but ties the money up for longer than the company is willing to wait
The NPV must be wrong, because a project cannot create value if it fails its payback target
It should be rejected, because payback is the more reliable of the two tests
The two tests always agree, so one of the calculations contains an error
check.question: The project above has a discounted payback of 4.66 years against a 4-year target, and an NPV of ZMW1,967. What does that tell you?

blocks.text: The discounted payback period is how long the project takes to earn its money back in present-value terms — the point at which the discounted inflows have caught up with the initial cost. A project passes if it pays back within the company’s target, where the company has set one.
You find it by carrying the present values forward in a running total and watching for the year the balance turns positive.

blocks.note: The balance is still ZMW3,746 short at the end of year 4, and in surplus by the end of year 5 — so payback happens during year 5.

blocks.text: To pin down where in that year, assume the year-5 cash arrives evenly and take the fraction you still needed.
DPP  =  A  +  (B ÷ C)
where: A = the last full year in which the cumulative balance is still negative
B = the amount still outstanding at the end of year A, as a positive figure
C = the present value of the cash flow arriving in the following year

blocks.text: Here that is 4 + (3,746 ÷ 5,713) = 4.66 years. Against a target of 4 years, the project fails — while its NPV said accept. The two tests disagree because they measure different things, and only one of them is about value.

check.explain: Once the outlay is recovered the method stops counting, so a long, highly profitable tail is worth nothing to it. Ignoring the time value of money is the weakness of ordinary payback — discounting is precisely what this version fixes.
options: It ignores every cash flow that arrives after the payback point
It ignores the time value of money
It cannot be used when a project has cash flows in more than one year
It requires an estimate of the cost of capital, which NPV does not
check.question: What is the main weakness of discounted payback as an appraisal method?

blocks.text: Discounted payback is a real improvement on ordinary payback, because it counts the cost of the money while the project is waiting to break even. It still has the flaw that ordinary payback has: it stops counting the moment the money is back.

rows: Time until the outlay is recovered

blocks.text: Two projects can pay back on exactly the same day, and one of them can go on earning for another decade while the other stops dead. Payback cannot see the difference; NPV can. That is why NPV is the primary test and payback is a secondary one — a check on risk and liquidity rather than on whether the project is worth doing.

For a Zambian business the liquidity question is not a technicality. A firm carrying kwacha debt through a period of high interest rates may genuinely need its money back inside three years, whatever the NPV says about year eight.
NPV decides whether a project is worth doing. Payback decides whether the company can afford to wait.

sections.heading: What each test is good for

check.explain: The NPV is zero at 9%, and NPV falls as the discount rate rises — so at 13% it must be below zero. The project earns less than the money funding it costs.
options: Reject it — its NPV at 13% must be negative
Accept it — a positive IRR always means a project is worth doing
Reject it, but only if the discounted payback also fails
There is not enough information without knowing the size of the outlay
check.question: A conventional project has an IRR of 9%. The company’s cost of capital is 13%. What follows?

blocks.text: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which a project’s NPV is exactly zero — the rate at which the project just breaks even in present-value terms. It is a break-even test on the cost of money rather than on sales volume.
Because it is a rate, it comes with a decision rule that reads naturally to anyone running a business: borrow at 10%, earn 13%, take the project.

items: For a conventional project — money out first, then a run of inflows — accept it if the IRR is above the cost of capital.
Reject it if the IRR is below the cost of capital, because the project earns less than the money funding it costs.

blocks.text: That readability is the whole appeal of IRR, and it is why boards ask for it. A percentage can be compared against the bank’s lending rate without any further explanation, where an NPV of ZMW1,967 needs someone to say what it is 1,967 of.

check.explain: 5% + [32,000 ÷ (32,000 + 78,000)] × 5% = 5% + 1.45% = 6.45%. The NPV falls away steeply here, so the crossing point sits much closer to the lower rate than to the midpoint of 7.5%.
check.question: A project has an NPV of ZMW32,000 at 5% and an NPV of (ZMW78,000) at 10%. What is its IRR?

blocks.text: There is no way to solve for IRR directly by hand on a project with several years of cash flows. Instead you calculate the NPV at two rates — one that leaves it positive and one that pushes it negative — and read off the point in between where the line crosses zero.
Take the same ZMW24,000 project from the last step. At 10% its NPV was ZMW1,967. Run it again at 14%.
The NPV crossed from positive to negative somewhere between the two rates, so that is where the IRR sits.
IRR  =  A  +  [ a ÷ (a − b) ]  ×  (B − A)
where: A = the lower discount rate, the one giving a positive NPV
a = the NPV at rate A
B = the higher discount rate, the one giving a negative NPV
b = the NPV at rate B, which is a negative figure

blocks.text: Watch the sign. Because b is negative, subtracting it adds: a − b = 1,967 − (−554) = 2,521. That denominator is the total distance the NPV travelled between the two rates, and the numerator is how much of that distance had been covered by the time it reached zero.
Against a 10% cost of capital the project is accepted, which agrees with the positive NPV — as it must, since both are reading the same cash flows.
Interpolation draws a straight line between two NPVs. The real relationship is a curve, so the answer is close rather than exact — and the further apart the two rates, the rougher it gets.

check.explain: Each change of sign in the cash flows creates the possibility of another rate at which NPV equals zero. With two changes there can be two IRRs, and 'accept if the IRR exceeds the cost of capital' cannot be applied to two different numbers. NPV handles the same cash flows without any difficulty.
options: The cash flows change direction twice, so the project can have more than one IRR and the accept rule breaks down
The rehabilitation cost cannot be discounted, because it is an outflow rather than an inflow
IRR cannot be calculated for projects lasting more than five years
The IRR will be understated, because the final outflow is discounted most heavily
check.question: A copper project has an outflow in year 0, inflows in years 1 to 8, and a large rehabilitation outflow in year 9. What is the specific difficulty this creates for IRR?

blocks.text: IRR is the most widely quoted appraisal figure and the least reliable. Three problems, in rising order of seriousness.
The decision rule is not always clear cut

A project whose cash flows change direction more than once — an outflow, then inflows, then a large closure or restoration cost at the end — can have two IRRs, or more, or none at all. A mine with a rehabilitation obligation in its final year is the textbook case, and it is a common shape in Zambia. Told that a project has IRRs of 6% and 31%, the rule to accept when the IRR beats the cost of capital simply has no answer.
It is not the return on the project

IRR is routinely read as the return the project earns. It is not. The calculation assumes every cash flow the project throws off is immediately reinvested at the IRR itself for the rest of the project’s life. A project showing an IRR of 30% only earns 30% if the company really can find 30% homes for the cash as it arrives — and a company that could do that reliably would not need the project.
It does not compare projects

Because two projects can have different lives, different sizes and different reinvestment assumptions buried in their own IRRs, ranking them by IRR can put the wrong one first. A small project with a spectacular percentage can beat a large one that adds far more value, and the percentage gives you no way to see it.
Where NPV and IRR disagree about which project to take, NPV is right. IRR is reported because it communicates well, not because it decides well.

check.explain: The reinvestment assumption is the flaw. A project with a 30% IRR only delivers 30% if every kwacha it releases can be put back to work at 30%, which is rarely true. MIRR makes you state the achievable rate instead.
options: IRR assumes cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself; MIRR uses a reinvestment rate the company can actually achieve
IRR ignores the time value of money, while MIRR discounts properly
IRR cannot handle an initial outflow, whereas MIRR can
IRR gives an answer in kwacha, while MIRR gives a percentage
check.question: What does MIRR fix that IRR gets wrong?

blocks.text: MIRR keeps what is useful about IRR — a single percentage you can hold against the cost of borrowing — while removing the assumption that broke it. Instead of pretending cash is reinvested at the IRR, you state the rate at which the company can genuinely reinvest, and build the answer on that.
The method collapses the project into two numbers: what it costs today, and what it will be worth at the end.

items: Take every outflow and discount it back to year 0 at the cost of capital. That is the investment phase, PVCF.
Take every inflow and compound it forward to the final year at the reinvestment rate. That is the return phase, FVCF.
Find the annual rate that grows PVCF into FVCF over the project’s life.
Accept the project if that rate exceeds the cost of capital.

blocks.text: MIRR  =  ⁿ√( FVCF ÷ PVCF )  −  1
where: FVCF = the future value of the return phase, compounded to the final year at the reinvestment rate
PVCF = the present value of the investment phase, discounted at the cost of capital
n = the life of the project, in years

blocks.text: Two different rates appear in one calculation, and that is deliberate rather than sloppy. Money the company spends is funded at its cost of capital; money the company receives is put to work at whatever it can actually earn. Those are genuinely different rates, and IRR’s mistake was assuming they were the same.

The reinvestment rate is not needed separately; it is already inside the ZMW80 million.

Yes — the MIRR is about 12.5%, and the project returns ZMW30 million more than it cost

check.question: A project’s inflows compound to ZMW80 million by its final year, against an investment phase worth ZMW50 million today. The project runs for four years and the cost of capital is 14%. Should it be accepted?

blocks.text: Same ZMW24,000 project once more. The cost of capital is 10%, and the company can reinvest cash it receives at 12%. Compound each inflow forward to year 5 — a cash flow arriving in year 1 has four years left to grow, one arriving in year 5 has none.

total: Future value of the return phase

blocks.text: The investment phase is simply the ZMW24,000, already at year 0. So the whole project reduces to a single question: what annual rate turns ZMW24,000 today into ZMW43,459 in five years?
12.6% is comfortably above the 10% cost of capital, so the project is accepted. Set the three answers side by side and the pattern is worth keeping.

rows: Accept — on an assumption the company can meet

blocks.text: MIRR comes in below IRR, and it will whenever the reinvestment rate is below the IRR. That gap is the size of IRR’s flattery. Where a project shows an IRR far above anything the company could realistically earn on spare cash, expect MIRR to be a good deal lower — and to be the number worth trusting.
MIRR is always the more honest percentage. NPV is still the decision.
